big_idea: Each number has its own written form. We can read and write 0-20. Teens (11-19) need TWO digits.
learning_intention: We are learning to recognise and write the numbers from 0 to 20, paying special attention to the tricky teen numbers like 13 and 14 that sound a lot like 30 and 40 but look different on the page.
student_learning_goal: I can read and write the numbers from 0 to 20.
success_criteria: I can match a number card (e.g., 7) to a group of seven counting objects.
I can put the number cards 0–20 in order, even when 11, 12, 13 try to confuse me.
I can trace and then write at least five numbers between 0 and 20 on my own.
lesson_specific_materials: Number cards 0-20, one set per child (M4)
A 'teen poster' with 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 in large print, with a 'tens-frame + extras' icon under each
Tracing strips with dotted-line numerals 0-20, one strip per child
Sticky tape or pegs to clip ordered cards onto a clothesline at child height
A long piece of yarn or string strung across the carpet to act as the 'number clothesline' from 0 to 20
Anchor chart paper labelled 'Tricky Teens' with columns 13 / 30, 14 / 40, 15 / 50, 16 / 60, 17 / 70, 18 / 80, 19 / 90

minds_on.hook: Mae and Theo were writing down a new cookie recipe — but a gust of wind blew their number cards everywhere! They need OUR help to put the numbers back in order from 0 to 20 so they don't accidentally bake 30 cookies instead of 13.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet near the yarn 'clothesline'. Hold up a basket of number cards 0-20, all jumbled. 'Look, friends — Mae and Theo's recipe cards got blown out of order. The clothesline is empty. We need to peg every number from zero up to twenty, in the right order.

 But watch out — some numbers like to TRICK us. Listen: thirteen … thirty. Fourteen … forty. They sound almost the same. Today we are going to learn how to TELL THEM APART by looking at how they are WRITTEN.' Pull out card 13 and card 30. 'Thirteen has a 1 then a 3. Thirty has a 3 then a 0. Different LETTERS for different NUMBERS.' Tape the teen poster on the easel. 'These are the tricky teens — eleven through nineteen. They all start with a 1.' Then peg 0 on the far left of the clothesline. 'Who can come find ONE and peg it next?' Take volunteers for 0, 1, 2 to start the line.

Counting Crew refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'TEEN starts with a ONE — DECADE starts with the BIG! That's the Counting Crew job!'
student_actions: Sit in a half-circle facing the empty number clothesline.
Listen as the teacher demonstrates 13 vs. 30 with the poster.
Volunteer to peg one card on the clothesline when called.
Chant the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 … as each card is added so the order builds aloud.

steps.instruction: Set up three rotating stations. Station MATCH: a tray of number cards 0-20 mixed up beside small bowls — each bowl has a quantity (e.g., 7 paper bears, 13 cubes, 20 buttons). Children pick a card and find the matching bowl. Station ORDER: a child-height clothesline with pegs — children take a small set of cards (a 0-10 set OR an 11-20 set, depending on readiness) and clip them in order. Station TRACE: tracing strips and pencils — children trace each numeral 0-20, with extra-thick dotted lines on the teen numbers. Walk children through the rotation rules; each station gets ~6 minutes.
steps.teacher_prompt: Demonstrate one card at each station before letting children rotate. 'At MATCH, you pick a card and find the bowl that has THAT MANY. At ORDER, the cards have to go SMALLEST to BIGGEST on the clothesline. At TRACE, you put your pencil on the dot and follow the arrow.'

steps.instruction: Rotate every 6 minutes. After each rotation, ring a small bell or clap a 1-2-3 rhythm and have children move clockwise to the next station with their work-in-progress (tracing strip travels with them; cards stay at the station for the next group). Circulate during ORDER especially — that's where the tricky teens trip children up. When a child clips 13 between 30 and 14 (or anywhere wrong in the teen run), pause and ask: 'Look at the number BEFORE 13. What is it? And the number AFTER 13? Which is bigger?'
steps.teacher_prompt: At MATCH: 'Show me — does this card match this bowl? Let us count the bears together. One … two … three … four … five … six … seven. And the card says?' At TRACE: 'Start at the dot. Follow the arrow. The teen numbers always start with a ONE. So 13 is ONE then THREE.'

steps.instruction: Final 4 minutes: pull the whole class back to the long carpet clothesline. The MATCH and ORDER stations have produced a wall of evidence. Now play 'Tricky Teens Tap'. Hold up a number — say it aloud (e.g., 'fourteen!') — and children tap their head if they hear a teen, tap their feet if they hear something else. Then point to the teen poster and have children chorus the digits: 'one-four', 'one-five', 'one-six' …. This rapid review locks in the visual-auditory link.
steps.teacher_prompt: Vary your call: 'fifteen!', 'fifty!', 'twelve!', 'twenty!', 'eighteen!', 'eighty!'. Watch which children tap correctly without hesitation — those are secure on A6.3 for teens. Children who freeze on 'fifty vs. fifteen' need the small-group recovery from the expanded walkthrough.

differentiation.for_emerging: Emerging children stay in the 0-10 range at all three stations. Their MATCH bowls have 1-10 quantities only. Their ORDER cards are 0-10. Their TRACE strip is 0-10. They get the teen exposure at the whole-class moment but are not assessed on writing teens this lesson — that's a Lesson 5 stretch.
differentiation.for_extending: Extending children stretch beyond 20: at MATCH they can match any card up to 25 (extra cards added to the tray); at ORDER they can place 0-25 in sequence; at TRACE they can write 21, 22, 23 unsupported on the back of their strip. Some can also draw the 'tens-frame plus extras' picture under each teen on the poster.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Pre-teach the teen-name pattern: 'thirteen sounds like THREE-teen because it has a 3 in it. Fourteen sounds like FOUR-teen because it has a 4.' Use the linking-cube tens-stick (a tower of 10) plus loose cubes as a tactile model: 'one ten and three more is THIRTEEN'. Allow tracing in coloured marker so the digit shape stands out. Pair with a same-language partner if possible.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-PURCHASE PATH: skip the printed number cards, tracing strips, and yarn clothesline. Children become a HUMAN clothesline — 21 children stand in a line, each is one number 0-20; teacher calls a number; the matching child steps forward and air-traces their digit with their finger; the class echoes the digit names ('ONE-FOUR for fourteen'). For tens-stick: a small group of 10 children clump as one ten-stick; extras stand to the side. Whole lesson runs on bodies + air-tracing — no printed cards, no clothesline, no purchased linking cubes.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: (a) at MATCH, does the child match the card to a quantity by counting one-to-one, or do they recognise the numeral and just KNOW the quantity (the latter is secure A6.3)? (b) at ORDER, can the child sequence 0-10 cleanly, AND do they place 11-20 in correct order without flipping a teen? (c) at TRACE, does the child form digits left-to-right and top-to-bottom (correct stroke order), or are they 'drawing the shape' without direction? Stroke-order matters because reversed digits (Ɛ for 3, ƌ for 6) are common at K and need correction now.
formative_check.how_to_record: Class formative checklist with rows for each child and three columns: 'matches numeral to quantity 0-10', 'orders teens correctly', 'forms digits with correct stroke direction'. Plus a comments column for reversed digits or specific teens that confused (e.g., '13/14 swapped' or 'reverses 6'). Keep the tracing strips — they are evidence for the per-child portfolio.

discussion_prompts: Mae just asked us — when she writes 13, what TWO digits does she use? Show me with your fingers.
Theo is mixing up 14 and 40. How can we help him tell them apart? Look at the teen poster.
If I say a number out loud and you have to find it on the clothesline, what is the FIRST clue you look for? (Answer we want: 'the first digit — is it a 1?').
consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. s the Counting Crew job!' Then each child holds up a number card from their pocket as they leave and reads it aloud — first the digits ('one … three'), then the name ('thirteen'). Teacher tallies on the anchor chart who said it cleanly, who said the wrong name (e.g., '13' read as 'thirty'), and who needed the digit-by-digit prompt.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Per-child formative checklist with three indicators (matches numeral to quantity, orders teens correctly, forms digits with correct stroke). Tracing strips kept as portfolio evidence — the teen numbers are circled if formed correctly, marked with a sticky-flag if reversed or skipped. Photo of the long clothesline with all 0-20 cards in order at the end of class. Exit-routine tally showing which children read teens aloud cleanly versus needed prompts.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: A6.3 'identify and write numbers to 20' is the most concrete and observable expectation in the unit — every child either writes the digit or they don't. The formative tier is appropriate because Lesson 5 will revisit number identification (children read numerals when comparing groups), and the diagnostic-from-Lesson-1 plus the formative-from-here together feed the Mid-Unit Formative Reflection. Children flagged for digit reversals get a one-on-one tracing minute in the morning meeting before Lesson 4.

expanded_walkthrough.title: Repairing 'Thirty / Thirteen' confusion — using the digit count, not the sound (Sarama & Clements, 2009; Fuson, 1988; Clay, 1991)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A6.3 numeral identification 0-20, the hardest piece at K is the teen / decade confusion. 'Thirteen' and 'thirty' sound nearly identical to a five-year-old's ear, and both contain a 3, so the auditory channel alone cannot disambiguate them.

Fuson's (1988) Number Word Sequence work documents that English teen names are PHONOLOGICALLY UNUSUAL — 'thirteen' violates the place-value-sound alignment found in many languages where the same number reads as 'ten-three' (e.g., Mandarin). English K children must learn the teen names as semi-arbitrary labels, then later overlay the place-value structure. Until that overlay lands, teen and decade names are interchangeable in the child's auditory memory.

Sarama & Clements (2009) place numeral-quantity matching at a separate trajectory level from numeral recognition: a child can recognise the symbol 13 visually and STILL not know which quantity it stands for. The MATCH station and the tens-stick demo are engineered for the matching subskill specifically.

Clay's (1991) developmental work on early numeral and letter formation documents that K children form digits by tracing OUTLINE rather than by stroke direction — leading to reversed digits (Ɛ for 3, mirror-6 for 9). The TRACE station's emphasis on direction-of-stroke + the formative_check 'forms_digits_with_correct_stroke' column are specifically about catching these reversals at K, before they become entrenched habits in Grade 1.

Why this matters: a K child who exits unable to disambiguate 13/30 in print will fail Grade 1 number-line work, place-value, and money. The repair must be VISUAL: thirteen has TWO digits (1 and 3), thirty has TWO digits (3 and 0), but the order is different and the FIRST DIGIT is the clue.

Step 2 (circulate during ORDER) is where this confusion shows up — a child clips 30 in the teen run, or pulls a teen card and reads it as a decade. The script below shows exactly what to say, what to point at, and why the linking-cube tens-stick is the recovery tool.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: ORDER station has a clothesline at child height with pegs. The child has a 0-20 deck and is clipping cards in sequence. They have just clipped 12 then put 30 in the next slot (instead of 13). On a small table beside the clothesline sits a tens-stick (10 linking cubes pre-snapped together) plus a small pile of loose cubes. Teacher carries the formative checklist clipboard.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script: Crouch beside the child. Don't say 'that's wrong' — instead, say: 'Walk me through your line. What did you peg first?' They'll likely say 'zero, then one, then two …'. Let them go all the way to 12. 'And then?' They'll point at the 30 card. 'And the next one?' They'll probably hesitate. Now hold up the tens-stick of 10 linked cubes. 'This is TEN. One stick of ten cubes.' Add three loose cubes beside it. 'TEN and three more. Count them with me — ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen.' Pause. 'Thirteen is a TEEN — it starts with a TEN-stick and has THREE extras. Now look at the card you pegged.' Hold up the 30 card. 'The 30 card has a 3 first, then a 0. Three first means THREE tens-sticks. Let me show you.' Pull out three tens-sticks. 'THREE tens-sticks is THIRTY — way more than thirteen.' Set them side by side: thirteen (one tens-stick + 3 cubes) vs. thirty (three tens-sticks). The visual difference is enormous and unmistakable. 'Which one belongs after twelve on our clothesline — thirteen or thirty?' Wait. They'll usually pick thirteen now. 'Yes! And how do we WRITE thirteen?' Hold up the 13 card. 'One, then three. One ten-stick and three more.' Have them swap the 30 card for the 13 card. Now point at 14, 15, 16 still in the deck. 'Each of these starts with a ONE because each is a TEN-stick plus more. Pegging 14 next?' They peg 14. Continue together to 19. Tick the 'orders teens correctly' column with a small note: 'needed tens-stick re-show'. That's a flag for tomorrow's morning meeting — give them a 90-second tens-stick refresh before Lesson 4 starts.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Pegs 30 after 12, says 'thirteen' but reads the card as thirty when prompted — auditory/visual mismatch unresolved. Most common K starting point.
(Mid) After the tens-stick demo, swaps the card and continues correctly through 13 and 14 but stalls again at 15 — needs you to show the tens-stick + 5 cubes once more before the pattern locks.
(Strong) After ONE tens-stick demo, says 'oh — every teen is one ten-stick plus extras' and pegs all the way to 19 unsupported.
(Stretched) Volunteers: 'And twenty is TWO ten-sticks!' — generalises the tens-stick model beyond the teens. Note this child for the Lesson-5 stretch task on composing 20.
common_misconceptions: Thirty and thirteen are the same number. (Auditory similarity dominates; the child cannot yet use the written digits to disambiguate. Most common at K.)
Teens come AFTER decades. (Some children peg 30, 40, 50 between 10 and 20 because they sound 'more like teens than ones do'. The tens-stick demo is the only durable repair.)

The number 12 says 'one-two' so the next number must say 'one-three' which is 13 ✓ — but then 14 must say 'one-four' which they correctly write, BUT they READ it as 'fourteen' or 'forty' interchangeably. (Reading and writing diverge at this stage.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child reverses a digit (writes Ɛ for 3, mirrors 6/9, draws by outline rather than stroke direction — Clay 1991): pause and re-teach stroke order. Show the digit on the teen poster with arrows. Have child trace it large in the air with their whole arm before re-tracing on the strip. Repeat for the next 3 reversed digits. Tick 'forms_digits_with_correct_stroke' only when self-correcting on next attempt.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child puts decade card (30, 40) in the teen run on the clothesline (auditory-visual mismatch — Fuson 1988 phonologically-unusual teens): always show the tens-stick. Words like 'teen' and 'ty' don't carry meaning at K — but a ten-stick of cubes physically demonstrates ONE ten-stick (teen) vs many ten-sticks (decade). Lay out 1-stick + 3 cubes (thirteen) BESIDE 3 sticks (thirty); the visual difference is enormous. Decode rule: 'Is the FIRST digit a 1? Then it is a teen.'

DIAGNOSTIC C — child can recognise the numeral but not match it to a quantity (matches 13 card to 13 cubes ONLY by recounting — Sarama & Clements 2009 numeral-quantity-matching gap): pair the visual with chanted speech AND with cube-counting. After fixing one teen, have child chant '11, 12, 13, 14, 15' while pointing at each card AND each cube cluster (tens-stick + 1 extra, tens-stick + 2 extras, etc.). Rhythm + visual + count locks the matching link.

worksheet_brief.purpose: End-of-lesson consolidation. Children practise recognising, tracing, and writing numerals 0-20 with extra emphasis on the tricky teens 11-19. Captures formative-level evidence for A6.3 — every child produces a written record of which numerals they can form independently. Goes home as a take-home practice sheet ('Trace and read your numbers with a grown-up').

parts_outline.task: Match each number card on the left to the matching group of objects on the right. Draw a line.
Trace the dotted numerals 0-10. Then on the second row, write 0-10 on your own.
Tricky Teens! Trace each teen numeral 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. Beside each, draw ONE tens-stick and the right number of extra cubes.
